claim: Wfs1 mutant mice developed early retinal electrophysiological impairments followed by marked visual loss.
source: Herein, we showed that Wfs1 mutant mice developed early retinal electrophysiological impairments followed by marked visual loss.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pERG and fVEP recordings showing progressive impairments, and optomotor reflex measurements showing visual acuity loss.

claim: Axons and myelin disruption in the optic nerve preceded the degeneration of the retinal ganglion cell bodies in the retina.
source: Interestingly, axons and myelin disruption in the optic nerve preceded the degeneration of the retinal ganglion cell bodies in the retina.
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM analysis showing optic nerve damage at 8 months and RGC loss detected only at 12 months.

claim: Transcriptomics at pre-degenerative stage revealed the STAT3-dependent activation of proinflammatory glial markers.
source: Transcriptomics at pre-degenerative stage revealed the STAT3-dependent activation of proinflammatory glial markers with reduction of the homeostatic and pro-survival factors glutamine synthetase and BDNF.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing upregulation of inflammatory markers and western blot showing increased pSTAT3.

claim: Glutamine synthetase was reduced in Wfs1 mutant retinas.
source: Transcriptomics at pre-degenerative stage revealed the STAT3-dependent activation of proinflammatory glial markers with reduction of the homeostatic and pro-survival factors glutamine synthetase and BDNF.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and immunofluorescence data showing reduced GS levels.

claim: BDNF was reduced in Wfs1 mutant retinas.
source: Transcriptomics at pre-degenerative stage revealed the STAT3-dependent activation of proinflammatory glial markers with reduction of the homeostatic and pro-survival factors glutamine synthetase and BDNF.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing reduced Bdnf gene expression.

claim: Label-free comparative proteomics identified a significant reduction of the monocarboxylate transport isoform 1 (MCT1) and its partner basigin.
source: Furthermore, label-free comparative proteomics identified a significant reduction of the monocarboxylate transport isoform 1 (MCT1) and its partner basigin that are highly enriched on retinal glia and myelin-forming oligodendrocytes in optic nerve together with wolframin.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS proteomics data and confirmed by western blot analysis.

claim: MCT1 and basigin are highly enriched on retinal glia and myelin-forming oligodendrocytes in optic nerve together with wolframin.
source: Furthermore, label-free comparative proteomics identified a significant reduction of the monocarboxylate transport isoform 1 (MCT1) and its partner basigin that are highly enriched on retinal glia and myelin-forming oligodendrocytes in optic nerve together with wolframin.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence showing colocalization of MCT1 and wolframin with MBP in optic nerve, and scRNA-seq data showing expression patterns.

claim: Loss of MCT1 caused a failure in lactate transfer from glial to neuronal cell bodies and axons leading to a chronic hypometabolic state.
source: Loss of MCT1 caused a failure in lactate transfer from glial to neuronal cell bodies and axons leading to a chronic hypometabolic state.
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical measurements showing lactate accumulation and ATP reduction in Wfs1 mutant retinas and optic nerves.

claim: The bioenergetic impairment is occurring concurrently both within the axonal regions and cell bodies of the retinal ganglion cells.
source: Thus, this bioenergetic impairment is occurring concurrently both within the axonal regions and cell bodies of the retinal ganglion cells, selectively endangering their survival while impacting less on other retinal cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MCT1 loss affects both retinal glia (supporting RGC cell bodies) and optic nerve oligodendrocytes (supporting axons).

claim: The metabolic dysfunction occurs months before the frank RGC degeneration.
source: This metabolic dysfunction occurs months before the frank RGC degeneration suggesting an extended time-window for intervening with new therapeutic strategies focused on boosting retinal and optic nerve bioenergetics in WS1.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing MCT1 loss at 5 and 8 months while RGC loss is detected at 12 months.

claim: Wolfram syndrome 1 (WS1) is a rare genetic disorder caused by mutations in the WFS1 gene.
source: Wolfram syndrome 1 (WS1) is a rare genetic disorder caused by mutations in the WFS1 gene leading to a wide spectrum of clinical dysfunctions, among which blindness, diabetes, and neurological deficits are the most prominent.
evidence: This is established knowledge about WS1 etiology.

claim: WS1 leads to blindness, diabetes, and neurological deficits.
source: Wolfram syndrome 1 (WS1) is a rare genetic disorder caused by mutations in the WFS1 gene leading to a wide spectrum of clinical dysfunctions, among which blindness, diabetes, and neurological deficits are the most prominent.
evidence: This is established knowledge about WS1 clinical manifestations.

claim: WFS1 encodes for the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) resident transmembrane protein wolframin.
source: WFS1 encodes for the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) resident transmembrane protein wolframin with multiple functions in ER processes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the WFS1 gene product.

claim: The first clinical sign of WS1 is the development of non-autoimmune diabetes mellitus (DM) during infancy.
source: In most cases the first clinical sign is the development of non-autoimmune diabetes mellitus (DM) during infancy followed by optic atrophy (OA) which leads to progressive visual loss in adolescence progressing relentlessly to blindness in adulthood (Wolfram and Wagener, 1938; Barrett et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Optic atrophy (OA) follows diabetes mellitus in WS1 and leads to progressive visual loss in adolescence progressing to blindness in adulthood.
source: In most cases the first clinical sign is the development of non-autoimmune diabetes mellitus (DM) during infancy followed by optic atrophy (OA) which leads to progressive visual loss in adolescence progressing relentlessly to blindness in adulthood (Wolfram and Wagener, 1938; Barrett et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Interventions to arrest or delay the loss of sight in WS1 are lacking.
source: While DM symptoms are clinically treatable with antidiabetic therapies, interventions to arrest or delay the loss of sight are lacking (Urano, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature.

claim: WS1 patients might develop hearing loss, ataxia, epilepsy, and peripheral neuropathy.
source: Although concurrent DM and OA are pathognomonic for WS1, patients might develop additional serious neurological illnesses, most commonly hearing loss, ataxia, epilepsy, and peripheral neuropathy (Minton et al., 2003; Chaussenot et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Serious psychiatric disturbances have been described in WS1 patients including psychosis, episodes of severe depression, and impulsive/aggressive behavior.
source: Serious psychiatric disturbances have also been described in WS1 patients including psychosis, episodes of severe depression, and impulsive/aggressive behavior (Swift et al., 1990; Swift and Swift, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Optic atrophy in WS1 is caused by the selective loss of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and their axons in the optic nerve.
source: OA is caused by the selective loss of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and their axons in the optic nerve with a pattern of degeneration that mainly interests the central part of the optic tract rather than the periphery and is accompanied by different degrees of demyelination (Zmyslowska et al., 2019; Barboni et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: The pattern of degeneration in WS1 optic atrophy mainly affects the central part of the optic tract rather than the periphery.
source: OA is caused by the selective loss of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and their axons in the optic nerve with a pattern of degeneration that mainly interests the central part of the optic tract rather than the periphery and is accompanied by different degrees of demyelination (Zmyslowska et al., 2019; Barboni et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Optic atrophy in WS1 is accompanied by different degrees of demyelination.
source: OA is caused by the selective loss of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and their axons in the optic nerve with a pattern of degeneration that mainly interests the central part of the optic tract rather than the periphery and is accompanied by different degrees of demyelination (Zmyslowska et al., 2019; Barboni et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Neuroimaging studies revealed diffuse alterations in the gray and white matters of the brain in WS1 patients.
source: Noteworthy, neuroimaging studies revealed diffuse alterations in the gray and white matters of the brain with significant loss of volume of the brainstem and microstructure abnormalities and signs of degeneration of myelin (Lugar et al., 2016; Samara et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neuroimaging literature.

claim: WS1 patients show significant loss of volume of the brainstem.
source: Noteworthy, neuroimaging studies revealed diffuse alterations in the gray and white matters of the brain with significant loss of volume of the brainstem and microstructure abnormalities and signs of degeneration of myelin (Lugar et al., 2016; Samara et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neuroimaging literature.

claim: WS1 patients show microstructure abnormalities and signs of degeneration of myelin in the brain.
source: Noteworthy, neuroimaging studies revealed diffuse alterations in the gray and white matters of the brain with significant loss of volume of the brainstem and microstructure abnormalities and signs of degeneration of myelin (Lugar et al., 2016; Samara et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neuroimaging literature.

claim: Wolframin is a multi-transmembrane protein resident in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: The gene mutated in WS1 is WFS1 which encodes for a multi-transmembrane protein and resident in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) named wolframin (Inoue et al., 1998; Strom et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to molecular characterization studies.

claim: WFS1 gene loss induces ER stress-mediated apoptosis of insulin producing pancreatic β-cells.
source: Mounting evidence suggests that WFS1 gene loss induces ER stress-mediated apoptosis of insulin producing pancreatic β-cells with disruption of cellular calcium homeostasis (Fonseca et al., 2005; Fonseca et al., 2010; Riggs et al., 2005; Yamada et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to mechanistic studies.

claim: WFS1 gene loss disrupts cellular calcium homeostasis.
source: Mounting evidence suggests that WFS1 gene loss induces ER stress-mediated apoptosis of insulin producing pancreatic β-cells with disruption of cellular calcium homeostasis (Fonseca et al., 2005; Fonseca et al., 2010; Riggs et al., 2005; Yamada et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to mechanistic studies.

claim: Wolframin increases the Ca2+ uptake within the ER, partially through the regulation of the SERCA pump.
source: In particular, wolframin is able to increase the Ca2+ uptake within the ER, partially through the regulation of the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase SERCA pump (Zatyka et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a mechanistic study.

claim: Wolframin loss results in Ca2+ leakage from the ER with a simultaneous increase of its cytosolic concentration.
source: As a consequence, wolframin loss results in the Ca2+ leakage from the ER with a simultaneous increase of its cytosolic concentration, activation of the Ca2+-dependent protease calpain which, in turn, activates programmed apoptosis (Lu et al., 2014; Takei et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to mechanistic studies.

claim: Wolframin loss activates the Ca2+-dependent protease calpain which activates programmed apoptosis.
source: As a consequence, wolframin loss results in the Ca2+ leakage from the ER with a simultaneous increase of its cytosolic concentration, activation of the Ca2+-dependent protease calpain which, in turn, activates programmed apoptosis (Lu et al., 2014; Takei et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to mechanistic studies.

claim: Wolframin is required for the proper release of both insulin and neurotransmitters from the ER and their delivery to the cell periphery through assisted vesicle trafficking.
source: Moreover, recent findings have suggested that wolframin is required for the proper release of both insulin and neurotransmitters from the ER and their delivery to the cell periphery through assisted vesicle trafficking (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: WFS1 deficiency deranges the IP3R-mediated release by destabilizing the NCS1 protein.
source: In fact, WFS1 deficiency deranges the inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (IP3R)-mediated release by destabilizing the NCS1 protein and, thereby, leading to reduced Ca2+ uptake by the mitochondria with consequent functional impairments (Schlecker et al., 2006; Cagalinec et al., 2016; Angebault et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to mechanistic studies.

claim: WFS1 deficiency leads to reduced Ca2+ uptake by the mitochondria with consequent functional impairments.
source: In fact, WFS1 deficiency deranges the inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (IP3R)-mediated release by destabilizing the NCS1 protein and, thereby, leading to reduced Ca2+ uptake by the mitochondria with consequent functional impairments (Schlecker et al., 2006; Cagalinec et al., 2016; Angebault et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to mechanistic studies.

claim: Wolframin is enriched at the MAM sites.
source: Moreover, a recent study unveiled an enriched localization of wolframin at the MAM sites and in WS1 patient fibroblasts, wolframin deficiency correlated with MAMs loss and, therefore, with defective Ca2+ transfer from the ER to the mitochondria and their related dysfunctions (La Morgia et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: In WS1 patient fibroblasts, wolframin deficiency correlated with MAMs loss.
source: Moreover, a recent study unveiled an enriched localization of wolframin at the MAM sites and in WS1 patient fibroblasts, wolframin deficiency correlated with MAMs loss and, therefore, with defective Ca2+ transfer from the ER to the mitochondria and their related dysfunctions (La Morgia et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Wolframin deficiency leads to defective Ca2+ transfer from the ER to the mitochondria.
source: Moreover, a recent study unveiled an enriched localization of wolframin at the MAM sites and in WS1 patient fibroblasts, wolframin deficiency correlated with MAMs loss and, therefore, with defective Ca2+ transfer from the ER to the mitochondria and their related dysfunctions (La Morgia et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Pharmacological activation of the sigma-1 receptor (S1R) counteracts the functional alterations of MAMs due to wolframin deficiency.
source: Remarkably, pharmacological activation of the sigma-1 receptor (S1R), an ER-resident protein involved in calcium ion transfer, was shown to counteract the functional alterations of MAMs due to wolframin deficiency (Crouzier et al., 2022a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a pharmacological study.

claim: Different Wfs1 targeted mutant mouse and rat lines have been generated and showed to recapitulate the main cardinal pathological traits of the WS1 patients.
source: Different Wsf1 targeted mutant mouse and rat lines have been generated and showed to recapitulate the main cardinal pathological traits of the WS1 patients.
evidence: This is established knowledge about animal models of WS1.

claim: Zebrafish mutant lines for wfs1a and wfs1b showed retinal abnormalities and behavioral visual dysfunctions associated with ER stress and impaired UPR response.
source: Furthermore, zebrafish mutant lines for the two homologue genes wfs1a and wfs1b have been recently produced showing retinal abnormalities and behavioral visual dysfunctions associated with ER stress and impaired UPR response in both strains (Cairns et al., 2021; Crouzier et al., 2022b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to zebrafish model studies.

claim: Wfs1exon8del targeted mice showed diabetic glucose intolerance and anxious-like behaviors upon stressful environment exposure.
source: Between the mouse models, the neurological and behavioral alterations of the Wfs1exon8del targeted mice have been extensively characterized showing diabetic glucose intolerance and anxious-like behaviors upon stressful environment exposure (Kato et al., 2008; Luuk et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to mouse model characterization studies.

claim: A histopathological study reported some thinning of the retinal tissue with lower retinal thickness/longitudinal diameter ratio in 4 months old Wfs1-deficient mice.
source: Visual impairment in these mice is less characterized with only a histopathological study that reported some thinning of the retinal tissue with lower retinal thickness/longitudinal diameter ratio in 4 months old Wfs1-deficient mice (Waszczykowska et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a histopathological study.

claim: A mutant rat line was obtained through Wfs1 exon 5 disruption showing diabetes, optic atrophy, and neurodegeneration.
source: More recently, a mutant rat line was obtained through Wfs1 exon 5 disruption showing the hallmarks of WS1, with diabetes, optic atrophy, and neurodegeneration (Plaas et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a rat model study.

claim: Increase of ER stress levels was detected in mutant rat retina, brainstem and pancreas, coupled with a volumetric decrease in all these districts.
source: The increase of ER stress levels was detected in mutant retina, brainstem and pancreas, coupled with a volumetric decrease in all these districts.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a rat model study.

claim: Prolonged administration of GLP1-R agonists demonstrated beneficial effects in preventing diabetes, excitotoxicity, and ER stress in aged rats and delaying disease progression.
source: Prolonged administration of the glucagon like peptide 1 receptor (GLP1-R) agonists have demonstrated beneficial effects in preventing diabetes, excitotoxicity, and ER stress in aged rats and delaying disease progression (Toots et al., 2018; Seppa et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to therapeutic studies in rat models.

claim: Synergistic effects of GLP1-R agonist and the BDNF mimetic 7,8-DHF co-treatment showed neuroprotective capacity on rats' visual pathway rescuing visual activity.
source: Very recently the synergistic effects of GLP1-R agonist and the brain-derived neurotrophic factor mimetic 7,8-DHF co-treatment have shown neuroprotective capacity on rats' visual pathway rescuing visual activity (Seppa et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a therapeutic study in rat models.

claim: Chronic ER stress and autophagy alterations caused by Wfs1 loss results in the acceleration of Tau protein aggregation and relative pathology in mouse hippocampus.
source: Interestingly, chronic ER stress and autophagy alterations caused by Wfs1 loss results in the acceleration of Tau protein aggregation and relative pathology in mouse hippocampus suggesting a novel mechanism by which wolframin deficiency can lead to neurodegeneration (Delpech et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to mechanistic studies.

claim: pERG measurements were comparable between wild-type and Wfs1 mutant mice at 2 months of age.
source: Whilst pERG measurements were comparable between wild-type and Wfs1 mutant mice at 2 months of age (WT: 68±5; Wfs1-KO: 72±6; p<0.05), a prolonged implicit time, which refers to the interval between the stimulation and the peak of the negative response, was detected in 4 months old Wfs1-deficient animals (WT: 76±5; Wfs1-KO: 82±6; p<0.05) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by pERG measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A prolonged implicit time was detected in 4 months old Wfs1-deficient animals.
source: Whilst pERG measurements were comparable between wild-type and Wfs1 mutant mice at 2 months of age (WT: 68±5; Wfs1-KO: 72±6; p<0.05), a prolonged implicit time, which refers to the interval between the stimulation and the peak of the negative response, was detected in 4 months old Wfs1-deficient animals (WT: 76±5; Wfs1-KO: 82±6; p<0.05) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by pERG measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claim: RGC abnormalities became increasingly more pronounced in 8 and 12 months old Wfs1 mutant mice.
source: This early indication of RGC abnormalities became increasingly more pronounced in 8 (WT: 73 ± 6; Wfs1-KO: 83 ± 9; p < 0.05) and 12 (WT: 76 ± 5; Wfs1-KO: 85 ± 5; p < 0.0001) months old mutant mice, with the latter group that showed, beside a delayed response , also a significant PhNR amplitude decrease (WT: 11±2; Wfs1-KO: 8±2, p<0.0001) at the latest time period (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by pERG measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 12 months old Wfs1 mutant mice showed a significant PhNR amplitude decrease.
source: This early indication of RGC abnormalities became increasingly more pronounced in 8 (WT: 73 ± 6; Wfs1-KO: 83 ± 9; p < 0.05) and 12 (WT: 76 ± 5; Wfs1-KO: 85 ± 5; p < 0.0001) months old mutant mice, with the latter group that showed, beside a delayed response , also a significant PhNR amplitude decrease (WT: 11±2; Wfs1-KO: 8±2, p<0.0001) at the latest time period (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by pERG measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 2 and 4 months old Wfs1 mutant mice did not display detectable VEP alterations.
source: While 2 and 4 months old mutant mice did not display detectable VEP alterations, 8-month-old mutant mice displayed increased latencies (WT: 46±4; Wfs1-KO: 51±2, p<0.001), indicative of slower transmissions along the visual pathway (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by VEP measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 8-month-old Wfs1 mutant mice displayed increased VEP latencies, indicative of slower transmissions along the visual pathway.
source: While 2 and 4 months old mutant mice did not display detectable VEP alterations, 8-month-old mutant mice displayed increased latencies (WT: 46±4; Wfs1-KO: 51±2, p<0.001), indicative of slower transmissions along the visual pathway (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by VEP measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Both VEP amplitude and latency parameters were significantly affected in 12 months old Wfs1 mutant mice.
source: However, both VEP parameters were significantly affected as mouse age progressed to 12 months (VEP amplitude WT: 40±14; Wfs1-KO: 28±2; p<0.001; VEP latencies WT: 47±2; Wfs1-KO: 52±3, p<0.001) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by VEP measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Wfs1 mutant mice showed a progressive reduction in visual acuity with undetectable differences at 2 and 4 months of age.
source: Wfs1 mutant mice showed a progressive reduction in visual acuity with undetectable differences at 2 and 4 months of age while a significant loss was recorded at 8 months which markedly worsened 4 months later (4 months - WT: 0.40±0.5; Wfs1-KO 0.36±0.8 c/deg, 8 months - WT: 0.39±0.4; Wfs1-KO: 0.30±0.3 c/deg, p<0.05, 12 months - WT: 0.38±0.6; Wfs1-KO: 0.19±0.5 c/deg, p<0.01; Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by optomotor reflex measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A significant loss of visual acuity was recorded at 8 months in Wfs1 mutant mice which markedly worsened 4 months later.
source: Wfs1 mutant mice showed a progressive reduction in visual acuity with undetectable differences at 2 and 4 months of age while a significant loss was recorded at 8 months which markedly worsened 4 months later (4 months - WT: 0.40±0.5; Wfs1-KO 0.36±0.8 c/deg, 8 months - WT: 0.39±0.4; Wfs1-KO: 0.30±0.3 c/deg, p<0.05, 12 months - WT: 0.38±0.6; Wfs1-KO: 0.19±0.5 c/deg, p<0.01; Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by optomotor reflex measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The initial visual impairment in Wfs1 mutant mice is represented by RGC alterations in the retinal tissue followed by a delay of the visual stimulus along the nerve fibers.
source: These results imply that the initial visual impairment in Wfs1 mutant mice is represented by RCG alterations in the retinal tissue followed by a delay of the visual stimulus along the nerve fibers suggesting a progressive optic nerve damage.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the temporal progression of pERG and VEP alterations.

claim: RGC functions are extensively altered causing a drastic loss of visual acuity at 12 months of age in Wfs1 mutant mice.
source: Subsequently, RGC functions are extensively altered causing a drastic loss of visual acuity at 12 months of age.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined pERG, VEP, and optomotor reflex data at 12 months.

claim: OCT and fluorescein angiography did not reveal any signs of retinal vasculature dysfunction in 8 months old Wfs1 mutant mice.
source: FA assessment was necessary to exclude confounding effects due to diabetic retinopathy (DM), which represents one of the major eye complications of DM but whose causative mechanisms are highly different from those in WS1 (Hilson et al., 2009). The collected images did not reveal any signs of retinal vasculature dysfunction in either group of animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by OCT and FA imaging shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: OCT-angiography did not highlight any significant difference in the eye fundi or perfusion and vessel length density and tortuosity in 8 months old Wfs1 mutant mice.
source: Indeed, OCT-angiography did not highlight any significant difference in the eye fundi or perfusion and vessel length density and tortuosity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by OCT-angiography data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant differences in RNFL thickness were disclosed by structural OCT in 8 months old Wfs1 mutant mice.
source: Moreover, we also assessed the thickness of retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL), and no significant differences were disclosed by structural OCT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by OCT measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Three 12 months old Wfs1 mutant mice did not show big abnormalities in RNFL thickness at OCT segmentation.
source: Since mutant elderly mice often displayed corneal haze, with consequent poor quality images, we managed to sample only three 12 months old clear-lensed eyes that still did not show big abnormalities in RNFL thickness at OCT segmentation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by OCT measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 8 months old Wfs1 mutant optic nerves presented incipient myelin thinning with reduced myelin area and a higher proportion of empty space, but without axonal count discrepancies.
source: These elaborations revealed that 8 months old Wfs1 mutant optic nerves presented incipient myelin thinning (g-ratio - WT: 0.52±0.18; Wfs1-KO: 0.54±0.14, p<0.05) with reduced myelin area and a higher proportion of empty space, but without axonal count discrepancies (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TEM imaging in 12 months old Wfs1 mutant animals unveiled signs of more severe myelin degeneration with pathological features and degenerating fibers.
source: TEM imaging in elderly mutant animals (12 months of age) unveiled signs of more severe myelin degeneration (g-ratio - WT: 0.42±0.18; Wfs1-KO: 0.50±0,18, p<0.05) with pathological features and degenerating fibers (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 12 months old Wfs1 mutant optic nerves showed a significant reduction of axonal density and area occupied by myelin together with evident signs of axonal damage with increased g-ratio.
source: In particular, we observed a significant reduction of axonal density and area occupied by myelin together with evident signs of axonal damage with increased g-ratio (WT: 0.41±0.04; Wfs1-KO: 0.51±0.003, p<0.05; Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Myelin alterations and axonal thinning are the first pathological signs followed by manifested myelin degeneration and axonal loss in Wfs1 mutant optic nerves.
source: These results provide evidence that myelin alterations and axonal thinning are the first pathological signs followed by manifested myelin degeneration and axonal loss in Wfs1 mutant optic nerves.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the temporal progression of TEM findings at 8 and 12 months.

claim: The pathological progression in Wfs1 mutant optic nerves is perfectly matching the timeline of the visual functional deficits previously uncovered by electrophysiological recordings and the optomotor analysis.
source: This pathological progression is perfectly matching the timeline of the visual functional deficits previously uncovered by electrophysiological recordings and the optomotor analysis.
evidence: This claim is inferred by comparing the temporal progression of structural and functional deficits.

claim: Unbiased stereology counting did not reveal significant RGC number changes in 8 months old Wfs1 mutant mice.
source: Unbiased stereology counting did not reveal significant RGC number changes in 8 months old Wfs1 mutant mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RBPMS immunostaining and cell counting shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The loss of the RGC population became evident and statistically relevant at 12 months in Wfs1 mutant mice (28% ± 6% loss in Wfs1-KO vs WT retinas).
source: However, 4 months later the loss of the RGC population became evident and statistically relevant (28% ± 6% loss in Wfs1-KO vs WT retinas) indicating a progressive loss of RGC somata over time (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RBPMS immunostaining and cell counting shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Axonal damage and myelin degeneration anticipate the frank loss of RGC cell bodies in the retinas.
source: These results illustrate that axonal damage and myelin degeneration anticipate the frank loss of RGC cell bodies in the retinas, even if within a relative delayed time frame a severe loss of RGCs can be also detectable in the Wfs1-deficient retinas.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the temporal progression showing optic nerve damage at 8 months and RGC loss at 12 months.

claim: t-SNE analysis of the RNA-seq datasets confirmed the expected closer similarity and correlation between all mutant retinas in comparison to the analogous wild-type samples.
source: t-SNE analysis of the RNA-seq datasets confirmed the expected closer similarity and correlation between all mutant retinas in comparison to the analogous wild-type samples (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by t-SNE analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Computational analysis identified 396 genes differentially expressed (DEGs) in mutant retinas compared to the control counterparts, with a similar proportion of either up- or downregulated genes.
source: Computational analysis identified 396 genes differentially expressed (DEGs) in mutant retinas compared to the control counterparts, with a similar proportion of either up- or downregulated genes (Figure 3B), suggesting not profound transcriptome alterations but rather selective changes in mutant samples at this stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Gene enrichment analysis revealed many deregulated genes related to pathways like cell death, UPR response and protein folding.
source: Interestingly, gene enrichment analysis (Gene Ontology, GO) revealed many deregulated genes related to pathways like cell death, UPR response and protein folding (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: All pathways related to cell death, UPR response and protein folding were down-regulated in the mutant retinas.
source: Intriguingly, all these pathways were down-regulated in the mutant retinas, in line with the general assumption from literature that wolframin loss impairs the cellular stress-coping capacities.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis and is consistent with literature on wolframin function.

claim: Mutant retinas upregulated key genes of neuroinflammatory pathways.
source: On the contrary, mutant retinas upregulated key genes of neuroinflammatory pathways (Figure 3C) as those associated with reactive glial cells like, Gfap, Lcn2, Edn2, Alpk1, and C4 (Figure 3D; Liu et al., 2022; Linnerbauer et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: Genes associated with reactive glial cells like Gfap, Lcn2, Edn2, Alpk1, and C4 were upregulated in mutant retinas.
source: On the contrary, mutant retinas upregulated key genes of neuroinflammatory pathways (Figure 3C) as those associated with reactive glial cells like, Gfap, Lcn2, Edn2, Alpk1, and C4 (Figure 3D; Liu et al., 2022; Linnerbauer et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D and citations to literature.

claim: Immunocytochemical analysis confirmed the aberrant activation of the ER stress effectors ATF6 and CHOP in mutant retinal samples.
source: We, next, performed immunocytochemical analysis confirming the aberrant activation of the ER stress effectors ATF6 (WT: 0.5±0.3; Wfs1-KO: 1.5±0.2) and CHOP (WT: 0.2±0.01; Wfs1-KO: 0.4±0.02) in mutant retinal samples (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: GFAP staining was found strongly upregulated in mutant retinal Müller glia at both 8 and 12 months of age.
source: Moreover, GFAP (8 months WT: 0.5±0.2; Wfs1-KO: 1.4±0.3; 12 months WT: 0.2±0.02; Wfs1-KO: 52±2) and Vimentin (VIM) (8 months WT: 20±2; Wfs1-KO: 38±5; 12 months WT: 2.2±0.5; Wfs1-KO: 4.6±0.8) staining was found strongly upregulated in mutant retinal Müller glia at both 8 and 12 months of age (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Vimentin (VIM) staining was found strongly upregulated in mutant retinal Müller glia at both 8 and 12 months of age.
source: Moreover, GFAP (8 months WT: 0.5±0.2; Wfs1-KO: 1.4±0.3; 12 months WT: 0.2±0.02; Wfs1-KO: 52±2) and Vimentin (VIM) (8 months WT: 20±2; Wfs1-KO: 38±5; 12 months WT: 2.2±0.5; Wfs1-KO: 4.6±0.8) staining was found strongly upregulated in mutant retinal Müller glia at both 8 and 12 months of age (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The glia-specific glutamine synthetase (GS) enzyme was found downregulated both at mRNA and protein levels in Wfs1-deficient retinas.
source: Furthermore, the glia-specific glutamine synthetase (GS) enzyme was found downregulated both at mRNA and protein levels in Wfs1-deficient retinas (Figures 3C and 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 3C and immunofluorescence data in Figure 4D.

claim: GS reduction in Wfs1-deficient retinal glial cells might favor a toxic environment detrimental for neuronal survival.
source: GS generates glutamine by assembling glutamate and ammonia and, therefore, having a critical role in preventing glutamate-dependent excitotoxicity and ammonia toxicity (Rose et al., 2013). Thus, GS reduction in Wfs1-deficient retinal glial cells might favor a toxic environment detrimental for neuronal survival.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the known function of GS and its reduction in mutant retinas.

claim: The genes encoding for the key neurotrophic molecule BDNF, and the survival factors Nr4a1 and Nr4a3 were reduced in Wfs1 mutant retinas.
source: Next, the genes encoding for the key neurotrophic molecule BDNF, and the survival factors Nr4a1 and Nr4a3 were also reduced in Wfs1 mutant retinas (Figure 3D), further altering neuronal homeostasis and stress resilience.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: BDNF is expressed by RGCs and Müller glia in adulthood retina, where it exerts its autocrine or paracrine effects.
source: In fact, BDNF is a well-known neurotrophic factor expressed by RGCs and Müller glia in adulthood retina, where it exerts its autocrine or paracrine effects.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BDNF expression and function in the retina.

claim: BDNF promotes survival of RGCs and can ameliorate RGC death after traumatic optic nerve injury.
source: Multiple lines of evidence suggest that BDNF promotes survival of RGCs and can ameliorates RGC death after traumatic optic nerve injury (Bennett et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature.

claim: Levels of interferon-inducible genes and NF-κB signaling components were unchanged in Wfs1 mutant retinas.
source: However, levels of interferon-inducible genes and NF-κB signaling components were unchanged suggesting the lack of a generalized inflammatory response, but rather a selective activation of specific neuro-inflammatory pathways.
evidence: This claim is inferred from RNA-seq data showing selective upregulation of inflammatory genes.

claim: RT-qPCR analysis on independent biological samples substantially confirmed the transcriptome data for the key selected genes.
source: To further strengthen our results, RT-qPCR analysis were performed on independent biological samples and substantially confirmed the transcriptome data for the key selected genes (Figure 3E), further highlighting a selective pro-inflammatory profile in Wfs1-deficient retinas.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The dysregulated Lcn2 and Vim genes in Wfs1 mutant samples have been shown to be direct targets of the STAT3 signaling.
source: On this line, we noted that the dysregulated Lcn2 and Vim genes in Wsf1 mutant samples have been shown to be direct targets of the STAT3 signaling (Herrmann et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature.

claim: STAT3 can be stimulated by the ER stress-dependent PERK and IRE1α pathways in glial and cancer cells.
source: Intriguingly, previous studies reported that STAT3 can be stimulated by the ER stress-dependent PERK and IRE1α pathways in glial and cancer cells (Meares et al., 2014; Chen and Zhang, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature.

claim: The active STAT3 variant (pY705) was highly enhanced in Wfs1 mutant retinal samples.
source: Interestingly, the active STAT3 variant was highly enhanced in mutant samples although with some variability among the samples (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: STAT3 regulated genes such as Fgf2, Il6, Vegfa, C1s, and C1rl were consistently upregulated in Wfs1 mutant retinas.
source: Thus, we profiled by candidate gene expression other STAT3 regulated genes such as Fgf2, Il6, Vegfa, C1s, and C1rl finding them consistently upregulated in Wfs1 mutant retinas (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A prominent pro-inflammatory molecular program associated with reduction of survival and homeostatic factors is promoted at least in part by the ER stress-dependent STAT3 activation in Wfs1 mutant retinas.
source: Altogether, these findings uncovered a prominent pro-inflammatory molecular program associated with reduction of survival and homeostatic factors which is promoted at least in part by the ER stress-dependent STAT3 activation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data showing ER stress, STAT3 activation, and inflammatory gene upregulation.

claim: Label-free LC-MS comparative proteomics identified 2046 proteins in retinal samples.
source: Overall, 2046 proteins were identified (Supplementary file 1) and the virtual 2D map showed the ability of the shotgun approach to identify proteins in a wide range of molecular weight and isoelectrical point (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The quantitative analysis led to the identification of 21 differentially expressed proteins between the two genotypes with 9 upregulated and 12 downregulated in the Wfs1-KO compared to the WT condition.
source: The quantitative analysis, combined with statistical evaluation, led to the identification of 21 differentially expressed proteins between the two genotypes with 9 upregulated and 12 downregulated in the Wfs1-KO compared to the WT condition (Figure 6B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The most upregulated protein upon Wfs1 gene loss was GFAP.
source: Notably, the most upregulated protein upon Wfs1 gene loss was GFAP, confirming increased gliosis described earlier in the mutant retinas (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Among the most downregulated molecules in mutant samples, MCT1 (Slc16a1) and basigin were identified.
source: Conversely, among the most downregulated molecules in mutant samples, we identified MCT1 (Slc16a1) and basigin.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: MCT1 belongs to the family of monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs) that promotes the transport across cell membranes and the shuttling between cells of energy metabolites as lactate, pyruvate or ketone bodies.
source: MCT1 belongs to the family of monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs) that promotes the transport across cell membranes and the shuttling between cells of energy metabolites as lactate, pyruvate or ketone bodies (Felmlee et al., 2020; Bosshart et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MCT1 function supported by citations.

claim: Basigin is a glycoprotein which assembles with MCT1 promoting its trafficking from ER and its stabilization on the cell membrane.
source: Basigin (known also as CD147) is a glycoprotein which assembles with MCT1 promoting its trafficking from ER and its stabilization on the cell membrane (Kirk et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about basigin function supported by citation.

claim: In brain, MCTs govern the extracellular release of lactate from glycolytic astrocytes and its transfer into neurons where it is oxidized to generate ATP.
source: In brain, MCTs govern the extracellular release of lactate from glycolytic astrocytes and its transfer into neurons where it is oxidized to generate ATP (Brooks, 2018; Magistretti and Allaman, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle supported by citations.

claim: Western blotting confirmed a strong downregulation of MCT1 in Wfs1 mutant retinas both at 5 and 8 months of age.
source: To confirm the proteomics results, western blotting for MCT1 was performed on independent retinal tissue samples confirming a strong downregulation of this transporter both at 5 and 8 months of age (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: A marked reduction of basigin was detectable in mutant retinas at 5 months of age.
source: Similarly, a marked reduction of basigin was detectable in mutant retinas at 5 months of age (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: MCT2 levels were found upregulated in 8 months old mutant retinas.
source: In contrast, MCT2 levels were found upregulated in 8 months old mutant retinas (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Loss of MCT1 and basigin is detectable months in advance respect to the frank degeneration.
source: Thus, loss of MCT1 and basigin is detectable months in advance respect to the frank degeneration suggesting that the pathological process proceeds with a relatively slow progression before leading to clinically relevant symptoms.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MCT1/basigin loss occurs at 5-8 months while RGC loss occurs at 12 months.

claim: MCT1 loss was detectable also in brain cortical and striatal tissue samples in 8 months old Wfs1-deficient mice.
source: Intriguingly, MCT1 loss was detectable also in brain cortical and striatal tissue samples in 8 months old Wfs1-deficient mice (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: MCT1 protein levels were strongly downregulated in WFS1-deficient HeLa cells.
source: Interestingly, MCT1 protein levels were strongly downregulated in WFS1-deficient HeLa cells, but not in equivalent cells that underwent the same technical procedures but without the successful inactivation of WFS1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data in WFS1 knockout HeLa cells shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The wolframin-dependent regulation of MCT1 protein levels is not restricted only to the retina but is a more general phenomenon.
source: These results suggest that the wolframin-dependent regulation of MCT1 protein levels is not restricted only to the retina but is a more general phenomenon.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MCT1 is reduced in both retina and brain, and in HeLa cells upon WFS1 knockout.

claim: MCT1-V5 was efficiently retrieved from the Wfs1-mCherry immunoprecipitated samples indicating that the two proteins can interact together.
source: Interestingly, MCT1-V5 was efficiently retrieved from the Wfs1-mCherry immunoprecipitated samples indicating that the two proteins can interact together (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Wfs1 and Slc16a1 were found predominantly co-expressed in glial and photoreceptor cells.
source: Interestingly, Wfs1 and Slc16a1 were found predominantly co-expressed in glial and photoreceptor cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Expression of Slc16a7, encoding for MCT2, was restricted to the retinal neuronal lineage.
source: Conversely, expression of Slc16a7, encoding for MCT2, was restricted to the retinal neuronal lineage similarly to its selective cell type expression in the brain (Figure 7A; Pierre and Pellerin, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 7A and citation to literature.

claim: Both wolframin and MCT1 proteins were detectable in lysates of isolated optic nerves.
source: We also confirmed that both wolframin and MCT1 proteins were detectable in lysates of isolated optic nerves (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Wolframin and MCT1 were mainly localized in MBP positive oligodendrocytes wrapping the axonal fibers.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis on optic nerve sections revealed that wolframin and MCT1 were mainly localized in MBP positive oligodendrocytes wrapping the axonal fibers (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myelin sheaths play a key role in glial-axonal metabolic support by shuttling metabolites like lactate and pyruvate toward axons to fuel the local energy demand.
source: Seminal findings have shown that myelin sheaths play a key role in glial-axonal metabolic support by shuttling metabolites like lactate and pyruvate toward axons to fuel the local energy demand (Fünfschilling et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to seminal studies.

claim: This trophic support is mediated by both MCT1 and MCT2 localized into oligodendroglia and axons, respectively.
source: This trophic support is mediated by both MCT1 and MCT2 localized into oligodendroglia and axons, respectively (Halestrap and Price, 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: MCT1 specific inactivation in oligodendrocytes or Schwann cells leads to late-onset axonal degeneration.
source: This process is crucial for energy homeostasis since MCT1 specific inactivation in oligodendrocytes or Schwann cells leads to late-onset axonal degeneration (Jha et al., 2020; Philips et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing the consequences of MCT1 loss.

claim: Wfs1 gene loss might affect MCT1 protein levels in the optic nerve myelin and the transfer of lactate within the axonal tracts.
source: Thus, it is plausible that Wfs1 gene loss might affect MCT1 protein levels in the optic nerve myelin and the transfer of lactate within the axonal tracts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed MCT1 reduction and its known function in lactate transfer.

claim: Lactate should accumulate in oligoglial cells that are not able to metabolize themselves the large intracellular quantities if MCT1 is lost.
source: If this is the case, it is expected that lactate should accumulate in oligoglial cells that are not able to metabolize themselves the large intracellular quantities.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the known function of MCT1 in lactate export.

claim: Biochemical quantifications showed a prominent accumulation of lactate in Wfs1 mutant retinas and optic nerves.
source: Biochemical quantifications in both retinas and isolated optic nerves showed a prominent accumulation of lactate in Wfs1 mutant samples (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by lactate measurements shown in Figure 7D.

claim: ATP levels were found significantly downregulated in Wfs1 mutant optic nerve and retinal lysates.
source: In fact, ATP levels were found significantly downregulated in Wfs1 mutant optic nerve and retinal lysates (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATP measurements shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Both Wfs1-deficient cell bodies and axons of RGCs are concurrently deprived of a key energy metabolite due to the failure to traffic lactate outside the oligoglial cells.
source: Given the failure to traffic lactate outside the oligoglial cells, both Wfs1-deficient cell bodies and axons of RGCs are concurrently deprived of a key energy metabolite.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed lactate accumulation and ATP reduction in both retina and optic nerve.

claim: Wolframin has a key role in maintaining physiological levels of MCT1 on glial cells to support the correct transfer of energy metabolites both within cell bodies and axons of RGCs.
source: Thus, these findings unveil a key role of wolframin in maintaining physiological levels of MCT1 on glial cells to support the correct transfer of energy metabolites both within cell bodies and axons of RGCs (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data showing MCT1 loss, lactate accumulation, and ATP reduction upon Wfs1 loss.

claim: The simultaneously loss of MCT1-dependent lactate transfer from glial cells to cell bodies and axons of RGCs represent a key pathological event which predominantly undermine the survival of this specific retinal cell type in Wfs1 mutant animals.
source: Thus, we postulate that the simultaneously loss of MCT1-dependent lactate transfer from glial cells to cell bodies and axons of RGCs represent a key pathological event which predominantly undermine the survival of this specific retinal cell type in Wfs1 mutant animals.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that RGCs have unique metabolic demands due to their long myelinated axons.

claim: RGCs have much higher metabolic needs respect to retinal interneurons that feature short-distance and unmyelinated projections contained within the retina.
source: Among all retinal neurons, RGCs are the unique neuronal cells with myelinated axons that travel long distances within the optic nerve to reach their brain targets. Thus, these neurons are predicted to have much higher metabolic needs respect to retinal interneurons that feature short-distance and unmyelinated projections contained within the retina.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the anatomical differences between RGCs and other retinal neurons.

claim: Mice with only one MCT1 gene copy develop axonal degeneration by 8 months of age.
source: On this view, mice with only one MCT1 gene copy develop axonal degeneration by 8 months of age and selective MCT1 inactivation in oligodendrocytes causes axonal injury (Lee et al., 2012; Philips et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to mouse genetic studies.

claim: Selective MCT1 inactivation in oligodendrocytes causes axonal injury.
source: On this view, mice with only one MCT1 gene copy develop axonal degeneration by 8 months of age and selective MCT1 inactivation in oligodendrocytes causes axonal injury (Lee et al., 2012; Philips et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to mouse genetic studies.

claim: MCT1 expression alterations have been observed in human neurodegenerative disease.
source: Thus, these results in mouse together with observations of MCT1 expression alterations in human neurodegenerative disease (Lee et al., 2012; Andres Benito et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2019), strongly point to MCT1-dependent bioenergetic loss as causative for neuronal function alterations and neurodegeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human disease studies.

claim: MCT1-dependent bioenergetic loss is causative for neuronal function alterations and neurodegeneration.
source: Thus, these results in mouse together with observations of MCT1 expression alterations in human neurodegenerative disease (Lee et al., 2012; Andres Benito et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2019), strongly point to MCT1-dependent bioenergetic loss as causative for neuronal function alterations and neurodegeneration.
evidence: This claim is inferred from mouse genetic studies and human disease observations.

claim: The first detectable pathological sign in Wfs1 mutant animals is the myelin derangement in the optic nerve.
source: Although we described metabolic alterations both in retina and optic nerve in Wfs1 mutant animals, the first detectable pathological sign is the myelin derangement in the optic nerve.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the temporal progression of pathological changes showing optic nerve damage before RGC loss.

claim: The optic nerve damage and axonal functional impairment likely represent the initial pathological defects caused by Wfs1 deficiency.
source: These observations indicate that the optic nerve damage and axonal functional impairment likely represent the initial pathological defects caused by Wfs1 deficiency.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the temporal progression of pathological changes.

claim: In WS1 patients the RNFL thickness shows a fast decline since early age which precedes of about a decade the atrophy of the cellular bodies of RGCs.
source: Remarkably, Barboni et al., 2022 have recently described that in WS1 patients the RNFL thickness shows a fast decline since early age which precedes of about a decade the atrophy of the cellular bodies of RGCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent clinical study.

claim: Experimental findings in mice and patients converge in highlighting RGC axonal damage as the first disease sign in WS1.
source: Thus, experimental findings in mice and patients converge in highlighting RGC axonal damage as the first disease sign in WS1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the convergence of mouse and human data showing early axonal damage.

claim: Chronic bioenergetic failure is an unprecedented new pathological mechanism at the basis of the selective loss of RGC responsible for visual loss in WS1.
source: Moreover, our results uncover chronic bioenergetic failure as an unprecedented new pathological mechanism at the basis of the selective loss of RGC responsible for visual loss in WS1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the novel findings of MCT1 loss and metabolic dysfunction in Wfs1 mutant mice.

claim: Neuroinflammation and MCT1-dependent energy insufficiency represent likely two independent phenomena triggered by separate Wfs1 dependent pathways.
source: Neuroinflammation and MCT1-dependent energy insufficiency represent likely two independent phenomena triggered by separate Wfs1 dependent pathways.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the relationship between two observed phenomena.

claim: Chronic inflammation causes a loss of astrocyte-oligodendrocyte gap junctions.
source: However, chronic inflammation causes a loss of astrocyte-oligodendrocyte gap junctions (Markoullis et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature.

claim: Astrocyte-oligodendrocyte gap junctions enable the shuttle of glucose from the blood circulation to oligodendrocytes through astrocyte intermediates.
source: These intercellular gap junctions enable the shuttle of glucose from the blood circulation to oligodendrocytes through astrocyte intermediates (Wasseff and Scherer, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature.

claim: Astrocytosis can reduce glucose availability in oligodendrocytes and consequently its metabolic support to axons.
source: Thus, astrocytosis can reduce glucose availability in oligodendrocytes and consequently its metabolic support to axons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the known effects of inflammation on gap junctions and glucose transfer.

claim: MCT1 downregulation and astrocytosis create a pathological axis that synergistically impairs oligodendrocyte metabolic support capabilities.
source: On this view, MCT1 downregulation and astrocytosis create a pathological axis that synergistically impairs oligodendrocyte metabolic support capabilities.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the synergistic effects of two pathological processes.

claim: Wolframin directs vesicle trafficking from ER to the cell periphery and this function can sustain the delivery of specific client proteins (i.e. MCT1 and basigin) to the cell membrane.
source: First, wolframin was shown to direct vesicle trafficking from ER to the cell periphery and this function can sustain the delivery of specific client proteins (i.e. MCT1 and basigin) to the cell membrane.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism of MCT1 loss based on known wolframin functions.

claim: Wolframin can stabilize MCT1 and basigin on the membrane and therefore protect them from selective degradation.
source: Second, wolframin can stabilize MCT1 and basigin on the membrane and therefore protect them from selective degradation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism of MCT1 loss.

claim: Wolframin-dependent ER stress might particularly affect the stability of selective proteins.
source: Finally, wolframin-dependent ER stress might particularly affect the stability of selective proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism of MCT1 loss.

claim: Wolframin has a general facilitatory role in the assembly of oligomeric protein assemblies.
source: An additional hypothesis is that wolframin has a general facilitatory role in the assembly of oligomeric protein assemblies. In fact, a previous study reported the concomitant loss of both alpha and beta-subunits of the Na+/K+ ATPase suggesting a possible role of wolframin in the correct folding and assembly of multimeric complexes in ER (Zatyka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citation to a study showing loss of another protein complex.

claim: Wolframin regulates MCT1/basigin protein processing and/or stability also outside the retina causing other symptoms associated with Wolfram syndrome.
source: Our results indicate that wolframin regulates MCT1/basigin protein processing and/or stability also outside the retina causing other symptoms associated with Wolfram syndrome.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MCT1 is reduced in brain as well as retina.

claim: MCT1 is strongly enriched in brain astrocytes and oligodendrocytes and sustain the lactate shuttle towards neuronal cells and their metabolic fitness and survival.
source: In fact, MCT1 is strongly enriched in brain astrocytes and oligodendrocytes and sustain the lactate shuttle towards neuronal cells and their metabolic fitness and survival (Fünfschilling et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MCT1 loss in the CNS might contribute to diffuse neurodegeneration underlying the progressive brain volume loss occurring in WS1 patients.
source: Thus, MCT1 loss in the CNS might contribute to diffuse neurodegeneration underlying the progressive brain volume loss occurring in WS1 patients.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the broader implications of MCT1 loss in WS1.

claim: MCT1 is the most abundantly expressed lactate transporter in peripheral nerves.
source: Finally, MTC1 is the most abundantly expressed lactate transporter in peripheral nerves and its inactivation in Schwann cells leads to hypomyelination and functional deficits in sensory, but not motor, peripheral nerves (Jha et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature.

claim: MCT1 inactivation in Schwann cells leads to hypomyelination and functional deficits in sensory, but not motor, peripheral nerves.
source: Finally, MTC1 is the most abundantly expressed lactate transporter in peripheral nerves and its inactivation in Schwann cells leads to hypomyelination and functional deficits in sensory, but not motor, peripheral nerves (Jha et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature.

claim: WS1 patients might develop peripheral neuropathy with increased impairment of the sensory component.
source: Intriguingly, WS1 patients might develop peripheral neuropathy with increased impairment of the sensory component (Liu et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to clinical literature.

claim: Gene therapy approaches to express a functional Wfs1 gene copy in RGCs in Wfs1 mutant mice will not efficiently prevent RGC dysfunction and subsequent loss.
source: In fact, given the selective RGC loss, research activities are in progress to establish gene therapy approaches to express a functional Wfs1 gene copy in RGCs in Wfs1 mutant mice. However, given our results we expect that this design will not efficiently prevent RGC dysfunction and subsequent loss.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the implications for gene therapy based on the study findings.

claim: Wfs1 gene activity should be restored in glial cells of the retina and optic nerve in order to correct the trafficking of energy metabolites and sustain the bioenergetics of RGC cell bodies and axons.
source: In contrast, Wfs1 gene activity should be restored in glial cells of the retina and optic nerve in order to correct the trafficking of energy metabolites and sustain the bioenergetics of RGC cell bodies and axons.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about therapeutic strategy based on the study findings.

claim: These findings uncover unprecedented therapeutic directions for WS1 calling for the exploitation of pharmacological strategies for metabolic support based on boosting glucose alternative energy substrates.
source: Altogether, by revealing new pathophysiological mechanisms underlying visual loss in Wfs1 mutant mice these findings uncover unprecedented therapeutic directions for WS1 calling for the exploitation of pharmacological strategies for metabolic support based on boosting glucose alternative energy substrates (Camandola and Mattson, 2017; Beard et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about therapeutic implications supported by citations to relevant literature.
